transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Order of the Dry Saint [F-02].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the reed roofs of Hollowmoot's outskirts as you haul a borrowed skiff up to the Ashwater tollgate, its chains dripping rust-red into the flood. Torches gutter behind a slumped barricade of sandbags and old doors; two Warden sentries huddle under an oilcloth, crossbows more for show than confidence at this hour. Somewhere behind you in the punt, a stranger you pulled from the water an hour ago mutters in his sleep — a low, wordless tune that makes the hair on your arms rise. The Wardens haven't heard it yet. You have maybe a hundred yards of black water and torchlight between you and finding out what they'll do when they do.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Ho there! Bit of a night to be standing watch—the flood's climbing something fierce. Any word when they'll open the Causeway again?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra guides the skiff toward the torchlight with practiced ease, sitting tall in the bow. She raises a hand in greeting to the sentries, her voice bright and easy as the rain drums down. She's calling to them like she knows them—because she does. Act natural. Get closer. Keep them talking.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Easy now, friend. We're going to be fine—just keep quiet for me, yes?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock poles the skiff forward with steady urgency, leaning down to grip the stranger's shoulder and ground him. Her jaw is tight as she locks eyes on the Wardens' torchlight ahead. She's done business with these men before, and none of it was good. But she won't show them fear or hesitation. Whatever this man is, whoever pulled him from the water, he's in her care now. She moves the skiff forward like she owns this black water, like she's done this hundred times before.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Ashwater gate. Need high ground before the weather turns worse. Pulled this one from the water maybe an hour back.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow poles the skiff with practiced ease toward the torchlight, his movements deliberate and open. Behind him, Brack shifts uneasily at the bow, ears flat, a low growl rumbling under the rain. The stranger's muttering has quieted to almost nothing, but something about them still sets the hound's hackles on end. Yarrow keeps one hand on Brack's scruff, steadying them both while reading the water ahead and the two slumped sentries in their oilcloth. He knew these men once, before the disgrace, and he still carries that same bearing—the kind that says *I know what I'm doing here*.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Warden Sergeant Coy steps out from under the oilcloth at the sound of Yarrow's voice, squinting through the rain before recognition — old, complicated recognition — crosses his face. "Yarrow Weir-keeper... didn't figure to see you polling up out of the dark again." He waves the other sentry to lower his crossbow, but his eyes drift past you to the huddled shape in the skiff's bottom, and to Brack, whose growl hasn't let up. Petra's easy chatter about the toll and Caddock's steady hand on the stranger's shoulder buy you the yards you need — the skiff bumps up against the gate pilings, torchlight finally close enough to see faces clearly. Coy's gaze lingers a beat too long on the muttering man. "He sick?" he asks, flat, one hand drifting toward the chain-latch instead of away from it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Just pulled him from the water, Coy—he's half-drowned and tired, nothing more. You know how the storm gets everyone wound up tonight.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra leans forward with practiced ease, the manner of someone who grew up at this gate. Her hand drifts toward her passage token, a casual gesture of familiarity and trust that speaks volumes to Coy.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: He's been in that cold water too long, that's all. Needs warmth, needs dry. I know what drowning does to people, Sergeant—I've pulled them back from it before. Let us through and he'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock keeps her hand firm on the stranger's shoulder, her body between him and Coy, meeting the Warden's gaze without flinching. Her voice carries the weight of a woman who's delivered children in worse conditions than this and won't be questioned about it. She doesn't move the skiff back; she waits, steady as stone.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Found him in the dark water, Sergeant, singing like nothing I've heard before. Brack won't settle, and Brack knows the difference between drowning men and something worse. I don't know what he is, but he needs shelter and light.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow meets Coy's gaze steadily, one hand still on Brack's scruff. He keeps his shoulders open, unthreatening, but doesn't look away from the Warden Sergeant—the kind of straight dealing that's kept his word good even through disgrace. He lets Coy see the tension in Brack, the hound's refusal to settle, because that's honest. Whatever this stranger is, Yarrow isn't going to pretend otherwise.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Rapport: dice + - - -, invoking Hears the swarm-song before others do [PE-03] → Good (+3) vs Good (+3): TIE

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: This man needs help, Coy—let us pass. Petra straightens, jaw set, meeting the Warden's gaze directly.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra refuses the compel on 'A Fisher's Stilt Hut'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's gesture toward her old passage token nearly works — Coy's eyes soften half a second at the familiar motion, the practiced ease of a girl who grew up at this very gate. But the tie doesn't tip clean her way: as her hand drifts to the token, the stranger in the skiff's bottom stirs and the wordless tune rises just loud enough to carry over the rain, the swarm-song unmistakable now that everyone's listening for it. Coy's fingers, already on the chain-latch, go white-knuckled around it instead of falling away. Petra sets her jaw and pushes forward anyway rather than let the moment cost her the stilt hut she keeps dry above the flood — she pays for that refusal in coin the Wardens understand: Coy's grip doesn't loosen, and he takes one wary step back toward the barricade, calling low over his shoulder for the other sentry to bring a torch closer, "for a proper look." The gate hasn't shut. But it hasn't opened either, and now four sets of eyes — Coy's, the second sentry's, and whatever's listening in that black water — are fixed on the sleeping man's face.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Wake up! Come on, stop singing!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra doesn't hesitate—she's heard the swarm-song before, and she knows exactly what it means. She lunges forward, grabs the stranger's shoulder, and shakes him hard, trying to snap him out of the song's grip before Coy locks them out.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm leans forward slightly in the stern, his eyes fixed on the stranger's face in the torchlight. He watches the rhythm of the humming, his jaw tightening slightly. His hand finds the blessed herbs and iron at his belt—a familiar weight. He remains silent, waiting.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The swamp water scrambles people's minds, Sergeant. I've brought a hundred back from worse. Let us through and he'll be fine by sunrise.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock's hand stays firm on the stranger's shoulder. She meets Coy's eyes without flinching—the steady gaze of someone who knows what she's looking at, who's handled this a hundred times before. She doesn't move the skiff back. Doesn't soften. She simply holds her ground, letting her bearing do what words alone cannot: *I know what I'm doing here.*)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That's the swarm-song, Sergeant—he's touched. We get him inside where there's light and fire, or the blight spreads. Your gate's the wall now. Open it.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow keeps one hand steady on Brack's scruff, the other gripping his pole. He doesn't advance the skiff but doesn't retreat, meeting Coy's eyes with the kind of quiet certainty that comes from someone who knows this threat better than most. His voice is low and final—not urgent, but clear as an order from a man still accustomed to being heard when it matters. Brack's growl subsides to a low rumble, but the hound's ears stay flat, his body tense against Yarrow's leg. The message is unmistakable: Yarrow understands what's at stake, and if he's asking Coy to open that gate, there's a reason the old Warden should listen.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Athletics: dice 0 + 0 + → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's hand cracks across the stranger's cheek and he jerks upright with a gasp, the wordless tune dying in his throat mid-note like a snapped harp string. For one long breath the only sound is rain on oilcloth — then the man blinks, coughs up swamp water, and asks in a cracked, ordinary voice where he is. Whatever had its hook in him, it's let go, at least for now. Sergeant Coy's white knuckles finally loosen on the chain-latch; he lets out a breath he'd clearly been holding since the singing started, and mutters something about "just a fever-touched fool, not the sickness proper," more to convince himself than anyone else. He waves the second sentry's torch back and hauls the gate chain up hand over hand, the old iron groaning as it rises. "Get him dry, Yarrow, and get gone before I think better of this," Coy says, not quite meeting anyone's eyes — old loyalty winning out over duty, this once. The skiff slides through under the dripping chains, Hollowmoot's lantern-glow finally within reach, the stranger shivering and bewildered but alive, and very much still yours to answer for.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: My cousin Edren—he was learning the weir-craft with me before the flood took him. Before the waters rose too high, he asked me if we'd find out together what had gone wrong with the old channels. I promised him we would. Now he's here in the Death-House, and I read his name aloud every time I come, honoring that oath to him and to all the others who can't speak for themselves anymore.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I'm not moving this pole until every name that drowned here has been read aloud—not for the Wardens, not for anyone. Edren deserves to be remembered by more than silence and rain.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Duty to the Dead'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Shelter at Yarrow offers the Death-House on Hollowmoot's north stilts — a cramped, dry chapel-hut where he still guards the drowned bodies of the parish, refusing to let the flood take them unnamed. Rows of shrouded dead line the walls, and he insists they won't mind sharing their roof with the living for one night. hides What the Death-House actually hides is that it's already on the Wardens' burn-list — quietly marked days ago after a hive-touched corpse was found among the dead Yarrow tends, and the torch crew was only ever waiting on the rain to break before putting it to flame..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The Death-House squats on its north stilts above the flood, low and close, rain drumming a steady percussion on cedar shingles that have somehow stayed whole. Inside it's dry — blessedly, achingly dry — and Yarrow moves among the shrouded rows like a man in a church he built himself, murmuring names as he passes, hand brushing linen-wrapped shoulders. Edren's shroud sits nearest the door, and Yarrow says his name last, voice cracking only slightly. The dead don't smell of rot so much as brine and reed-must, and for a moment it's almost peaceful — until someone notices one shroud, near the back wall, tied differently than the rest, its ropes newer, its knots hurried. Outside, the rain has thinned to a drizzle, and somewhere down the causeway a bell that isn't Saint Orrin's begins, faintly, to toll — the kind of toll that means torches are being lit.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That's not Saint Orrin's bell—the Wardens' torch-crew! This place is marked for burning tonight, Yarrow. How many more names can you read before the fire comes?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's entire stance shifts at the unfamiliar bell-toll. Her hand moves to her pass-token by reflex, then drops. Her eyes are bright with the terrible knowledge of a girl raised among warnings. She's calculating—time, danger, the shrouded rows. She doesn't move to flee yet; she waits to see what Yarrow will do.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That knot-work is fresh. And listen—that bell. They're coming.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm's head snaps up at the distant bell toll. He crosses to the back wall where the differently-tied shroud lies, his movements precise and practiced. He leans in to examine the knots—newer rope, hastily wound—and traces the wrapping with practiced fingers, reading the corpse like scripture.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: That's a Warden bell. They're coming to burn this place. And that shroud there—one of the touched. They won't have it while I'm here.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock's head snaps up at the faint bell tolling down the causeway—not a saint's bell, not a funeral toll, but the sharp high call that means Wardens are lighting torches. She's heard it before. She strides to the back wall and kneels beside the shroud with the hastily-tied ropes, her weathered hands tracing the knots. When she looks up at Yarrow, her jaw is set.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That bell isn't for blessing the dead—it's the Wardens' mark for fire. And these knots... someone put this shroud here after the others, trying to hide what's underneath.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow strides back through the rows of shrouded dead to the rear wall, rain-damp and urgent. His weathered fingers trace the hasty knots—newer rope, tied in haste and fear, nothing like the careful reverence he laid across Edren. He works at the bindings, jaw tight. Outside, the tolling grows sharper. Torches bob at the base of the north stilts, and boots thud on the causeway planks, climbing fast.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I don't care if they're climbing the stilts right now—I won't leave this body to burn unnamed and forgotten. Not after they went to such trouble to hide it. Someone put this one here in secret, and that means *something*. That means it matters.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Investigate: dice - 0 - -, invoking Trained to purge the hive from flesh himself [AN-04] → Fair (+2) vs Fair (+2): TIE

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Holy ground. This body, this soul—they deserve blessing, not ash. I stand witness and guardian tonight, and no Warden torch crosses this threshold.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Burning Religious Zeal'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm's fingers work the hasty knots loose even as his reading falters — the rope binds oddly, doubled back on itself like whoever tied it was shaking. The shroud falls open at the shoulder, and there's no mistaking what's underneath: grey-veined skin, a wound gone black and weeping, features slack in the particular stillness of the hive-touched dead. Caddock is already on her knees beside it, murmuring something that isn't quite a prayer, one hand raised as if daring anyone to move the body. Outside, the bell stops. Boots hit the base of the north stilts — many boots — and torchlight flares orange through the seams in the shutters. A voice, young and scared and trying not to sound it, calls up through the rain: "Death-House! Warden business — open it or we burn it shut!" Yarrow's jaw sets. Edren's shroud is nearest the door. So is the hidden one.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: He mended the strap on my remedy satchel three winters back — asked nothing but to hear old mill stories. I've carried it every day since. Seeing him now, grey-veined and hollow... I don't know if this is Fennard with the hive puppeting his flesh, or if there's nothing left of him at all. Not knowing which eats at me worse than knowing he was gone.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That's Fennard the tinker — I knew him. But his voice carries, and the hive's song draws them. We have to move.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'A Travelling Tinker'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: The pack's leader is a face Anselm half-recognizes under the grey veining and matted hair: the travelling tinker who once mended half of Hollowmoot's pots and knew every road in the Sallowmere, now hive-touched and hollow-eyed, still clutching his battered tool-satchel as he wades out of the reeds at the head of the pack. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because The pack doesn't just want the party's food — they're driving them off the solid ford-line entirely, herding them toward the reed mats that hide the sucking mire beneath, where anyone dragged down won't come back up easy..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The reeds erupt on both banks at once — grey-veined shapes wading up out of the shallows with hooked spears, and at their head, unmistakable even hollowed-out and matted with filth, Fennard the tinker, tool-satchel still slung across his back like habit outlives everything else. He doesn't lunge for you so much as herd — spears snapping low and wide, forcing your footing off the packed stone of the ford and onto the deceptively flat mats of reed that Yarrow's people have always known to avoid. Rain sheets down, the swarm-song rises under the splash and grunt of the attack, and somewhere beneath those innocent green mats the mire waits, patient and bottomless. Anselm freezes half a heartbeat too long, staring into a face he mended a strap for three winters back — and that heartbeat is exactly the opening the pack needed.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Hold the line with me—there's stone beneath, I can hear it! Follow where I lead!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's ear for reading water levels picks out the rhythm beneath the chaos—the old pilings of the causeway still holding firm beneath the reed mat, their solid wood structure creating a true ford where the hive-touched expect only sucking mud. Even as the spears slash low, she sidesteps and positions herself between the pack and Anselm's frozen form, calling out the invisible landmarks.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Back!

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm snaps from his paralysis. His blade meets the hooked spears thrust from the reeds, turning them aside with the cold precision of someone trained to read and resist the hive's puppet-work in every motion. He steps forward to regain the solid stone of the ford.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Off the reeds! The stone holds—follow me to the solid ground, now!

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock moves with unshakeable purpose, her body reading the ground beneath her as surely as her hands read a woman in labor. She grabs whoever is closest—reaching, pulling—and hauls them bodily off the treacherous reed mat back toward the solid stone of the ford, her strength a lever against the closing spears.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: "The pilings! There — follow the marks I'm calling. This ground holds. Trust the old line."

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow plants his feet firm on solid stone, eyes tracking the water's flow and the subtle scar-marks where old pilings just beneath the surface guide the true ford. He's read these marks a hundred times in a hundred floods. He points, commanding: his voice cutting through rain and hive-song both, marking the solid ground, reading the old surveys his family carved into memory and moss. The pilings are still there. The firm ground is still there.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice - - + + → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — attack with Fight: dice - - 0 0, invoking walks every road [PX-08], Remembers the old mill-roads now underwater [AN-01], Trained to purge the hive from flesh himself [AN-04] → Fantastic (+6) vs Great (+4): SUCCESS (Fennard's Hive-Touched Pack stress 2)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — overcome with Physique: dice 0 - + - → Good (+3) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice + - + -, invoking Reads water-flow like other men read faces [YA-03] → Fantastic (+6) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Fennard's Hive-Touched Pack attacks Yarrow (physical): Good (+3) vs Yarrow's Athletics Superb (+5) — defended

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: It works. Petra's called landmarks and Yarrow's shouted line converge into one true path, and Caddock's grip on collars and cloaks drags everyone onto packed stone before the reed mats can swallow a single boot. Anselm shakes off the half-second where Fennard's ruined face held him frozen, and his blade answers the hooked spears with brutal precision — steel rings, a spearman staggers back clutching a torn arm, and for the first time the pack's herding rhythm breaks. Fennard himself flinches at the clash of steel, tool-satchel swinging wild, and something like recognition — or just pain — crosses that grey-veined face before he barks a wordless order and the pack melts back into the reeds, dragging their hurt with them, the swarm-song fading downstream. As the rain-scoured quiet settles, Yarrow's eyes catch on something past the retreating pack — a thread of smoke rising where no smoke should be, off toward a village that should be ringing its evening bell and isn't. The ford holds. The mire keeps its secrets a while longer.

transcript.text: Petra's fingers find the bell-ropes like she's done it a thousand times in dreams, and she pulls—not the frantic tolling of alarm, but Saint Orrin's old homecoming sequence, three slow strikes and a pause, the pattern etched into her bones since childhood. The homecoming bells' three-note sequence reverberates through the stairwell, bouncing off ancient stone, calling the boy home like a rope thrown into darkness. Beneath that bright peal, he catches it: the boy's voice still holding its own against the hive-song's hunger, thin but present, still *his own*. Yarrow's breathing stays level. But Petra's bells are louder here, right at the source, and the boy's true voice is right underneath them now, no longer buried. Caddock doesn't hesitate — she wraps him up the way she's caught a thousand newborns, steady hands, steady voice, murmuring "I've got you, I've got you" until his shaking stops. Yarrow holds the stair below with his spear, watching the dark for anything the song might still call up, but nothing comes; whatever else roosts in this tower, it lets this one go. Anselm reaches the belfry last and presses blessed salt into the fresh wound on the boy's arm before the hive can take root — his own hands, his own rites, no one else's, just as he swore. Down at the waterline Mother Wrenna sees them silhouetted against the tower's dark mouth and starts wading in before the skiff even touches stone, sobbing her son's name.
